overview: Two clinically important yeasts distinguished by morphology, capsule presence, and the immune status of patients typically affected.
genZNote: Candida sprouts a tail (germ tube). Cryptococcus wears a hazmat suit (capsule).

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A dimorphic yeast and normal commensal of mucosal surfaces that becomes pathogenic in disrupted flora or immunosuppression (candidiasis).
aspects.valueB: An encapsulated yeast found in soil and bird droppings that causes cryptococcosis, especially meningitis in immunocompromised hosts.

aspects.label: Capsule
aspects.valueB: Prominent polysaccharide capsule, visible with India ink preparation.

aspects.label: Morphology
aspects.valueA: Forms budding yeast, pseudohyphae, and true hyphae/germ tubes at 37°C.
aspects.valueB: Round to oval budding yeast; does not form hyphae in typical clinical presentation.

aspects.label: Key Identification Test
aspects.valueA: Germ tube test — positive within 2-3 hours in serum at 37°C.
aspects.valueB: India ink stain showing a clear halo (capsule) around the yeast; urease-positive.

aspects.label: Clinical Presentation
aspects.valueA: Oral thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis, invasive candidiasis/candidemia in hospitalized or immunosuppressed patients.
aspects.valueB: Cryptococcal meningitis (classically in AIDS patients), pulmonary cryptococcosis.

aspects.label: Diagnosis
aspects.valueA: Culture, germ tube test, and sometimes chromogenic agar for species identification.
aspects.valueB: India ink microscopy, cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) testing in serum/CSF, and culture on Sabouraud agar.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueB: Encapsulated, India ink positive, classic cause of fungal meningitis.
